units.title: Unit 03 — Grammatical categories of collocation
learningObjectives: Identify verb–noun, noun–verb, noun–noun, adjective–noun, adverb–adjective and longer collocation patterns.
Distinguish typical partners such as draw up a contract, an opportunity arises and a barrage of questions.
Choose precise collocations for intensification, physical actions and recurring events without unnatural substitutions.

items.example: The organiser drew up a list of participants before sending the invitations.
items.note: Draw up means prepare a written document or list, often systematically.

items.example: The legal team will draw up a contract once both parties agree on the price.
items.note: Draw up a contract means prepare its formal written terms, not simply sign it.

items.example: She refused to pass up a chance to present her research abroad.
items.note: Pass up a chance means choose not to use an opportunity that is available.

items.example: I would hate to pass up an opportunity to work with that research group.
items.note: An opportunity is something advantageous you could take; pass up means decline it.

items.example: The sealed enclosure must withstand pressure during the qualification tests.
items.note: Withstand means remain effective or intact despite pressure, stress or force.

items.example: The protective casing was designed to withstand the impact of falling equipment.
items.note: Use withstand the impact when something can endure a sudden physical force.

items.example: If an opportunity arises to study abroad, I will consider applying.
items.note: An opportunity arises rather than happens when a useful possibility becomes available.

items.example: Safety standards can slip when routine inspections are repeatedly postponed.
items.note: Standards slip when an established level of quality or performance gradually falls.

items.example: A spate of attacks prompted residents to request better street lighting.
items.note: A spate means several similar undesirable events occurring close together in time.

items.example: The museum reported a spate of thefts during the summer season.
items.note: Spate often combines with crimes or incidents occurring in quick succession.

items.example: After the announcement, the director faced a barrage of questions from employees.
items.note: A barrage of questions suggests numerous questions arriving rapidly and insistently.

items.example: The referee endured a barrage of insults from frustrated spectators.
items.note: Barrage conveys a forceful, continuous stream rather than a single insult.

items.example: By a stroke of luck, the missing sample turned up before the audit.
items.note: A stroke of luck is an unexpected fortunate event, not a prolonged success.

items.example: A snippet of information from an old report helped the team identify the defect.
items.note: Snippet refers to a very small piece of information or text.

items.example: The customer realised it was an idle threat when no complaint was filed.
items.note: An idle threat is not seriously intended or unlikely to be carried out.

items.example: They kept checking the old server in the vain hope of recovering the files.
items.note: Vain hope refers to a wish with little realistic chance of being fulfilled.

items.example: There is mounting concern about the reliability of the ageing equipment.
items.note: Mounting shows that concern is increasing over time, not remaining constant.

items.example: The proposal faced mounting criticism as more financial details became public.
items.note: Mounting criticism grows in volume or intensity as objections accumulate.

items.example: The unexplained service cuts caused mounting fury among local residents.
items.note: Mounting can intensify emotional nouns such as fury, criticism and concern.

items.example: The plain truth is that the team missed the deadline because the tests failed.
items.note: The plain truth introduces an unembellished fact, even if it is uncomfortable.

items.example: The simple truth is that we cannot finish the work without more staff.
items.note: The simple truth presents a straightforward explanation without complication.

items.example: Her memoir offers an intensely personal account of moving to a new country.
items.note: Intensely strengthens personal when feelings or experiences are deeply private.

items.example: The historic building looked stunningly attractive after its restoration.
items.note: Stunningly attractive expresses an exceptional impression of visual appeal.

items.example: The first attempt to automate the process failed miserably in testing.
items.note: Fail miserably signals very serious failure rather than a small setback.

items.example: Drivers who drive recklessly put pedestrians and cyclists at risk.
items.note: Recklessly describes driving without adequate regard for danger or consequences.

items.example: During the celebration, several colleagues burst into song without warning.
items.note: Burst into song means begin singing suddenly or spontaneously.

items.example: The vet examined the animal after it began to foam at the mouth.
items.note: This phrase describes visible froth at the mouth; it can be literal or figurative.

items.word: take it easy for a while
items.pt: descansar e pegar leve por um tempo
items.example: After the operation, the coach advised her to take it easy for a while.
items.note: Take it easy means avoid exertion or stress and rest temporarily.

items.example: You can acknowledge a mistake and still put the past behind you.
items.note: Put the past behind you means move on instead of being controlled by earlier events.

items.example: The health department acted quickly when the disease began to spread.
items.note: Diseases spread between people, animals or places; the noun is the subject.

items.example: Recent evidence suggests that the new process uses less energy.
items.note: Evidence suggests introduces a conclusion supported, but not necessarily proved, by data.

items.example: Dark smoke rises above the warehouse whenever the furnace starts.
items.note: Smoke rises naturally describes its upward movement through the air.

items.pt: os dentes batem de frio ou medo
items.example: His teeth began to chatter while he waited outside in the freezing rain.
items.note: Teeth chatter describes involuntary rapid movement caused by cold or fear.

items.example: At night the wind howls through the narrow streets of the village.
items.note: Howl presents a strong wind as making a loud, eerie sound.

items.example: A gentle breeze kept the outdoor meeting pleasantly cool.
items.note: Gentle combines with breeze to describe light, comfortable wind.

items.example: A strong wind forced the organisers to move the event indoors.
items.note: Strong wind is a natural pairing when describing substantial wind force.

units.title: Unit 04 — Finding and working on collocations in texts
learningObjectives: Notice useful word partnerships in journalistic, narrative and informational texts and record them accurately.
Extend a target word into families of stronger and more flexible combinations with chance, challenge, value and source.
Use natural collocations when discussing professional development, opportunities and independent vocabulary study.

items.example: The hospital recruited several newly qualified nurses for its training programme.
items.note: Newly qualified describes someone who has only recently gained professional credentials.

items.example: Small businesses must face the challenge of rising operating costs.
items.note: Face the challenge means confront a difficult demand rather than avoid it.

items.example: Designing an affordable prototype proved to be a tough challenge.
items.note: Tough intensifies challenge by emphasising its difficulty.

items.example: The new manager worked hard to gain her team's respect.
items.note: Gain someone's respect suggests earning esteem through your behaviour or achievements.

items.example: The campaign finally won the battle to secure safer working conditions.
items.note: Win the battle can describe overcoming a prolonged problem, literally or figuratively.

items.example: Only fully qualified technicians are authorised to perform this inspection.
items.note: Fully qualified means having all credentials or skills required for the role.

items.example: The appointment remains provisional pending the results of the background checks.
items.note: Pending means until something has been decided or become available; it sounds formal.

items.example: The research programme passed a milestone when its first prototype was approved.
items.note: A milestone is a significant stage reached in an ongoing process.

items.example: A steady income gave the family greater financial stability.
items.note: Financial stability is a sustained ability to meet financial commitments.

items.example: With the audit finished, you can turn your thoughts to the next release.
items.note: Turn your thoughts to means shift mental attention towards another matter.

items.example: His gift for languages helped him learn Italian remarkably quickly.
items.note: A gift for languages is natural aptitude, not a present given to someone.

items.example: Even a small software fix can make a difference to thousands of users.
items.note: Make a difference means have a meaningful effect, often a beneficial one.

items.example: The cause of the unusual signal remained an enigma for several months.
items.note: Remain an enigma means continue to be difficult to understand or explain.

items.example: The conference offered simultaneous translation for international delegates.
items.note: Simultaneous translation happens while the original speaker is talking.

items.example: The organisers hired specialists to provide simultaneous translation throughout the event.
items.note: Provide collocates with a service such as translation or interpretation.

items.example: The source of the intermittent fault was difficult to pin down.
items.note: Pin down means identify or describe something precisely despite uncertainty.

items.example: The town offered no-cost entertainment during the summer festival.
items.note: No-cost modifies entertainment to emphasise that there is no admission charge.

items.pt: um ambiente sem circulação de carros
items.example: The market took place in a car-free setting near the historic square.
items.note: A car-free setting is an area intended for people without regular motor traffic.

items.example: Never underestimate the value of clear documentation in a large project.
items.note: Underestimate the value of means fail to appreciate how helpful something is.

items.example: For the children, building small robots became a source of fun.
items.note: Source of combines with an abstract noun to name where that experience comes from.

items.example: The foundation paid a modest sum to rent the hall for the afternoon.
items.note: Modest sum refers to a relatively small amount of money.

items.example: The puppy's playful behaviour was a constant source of amusement.
items.note: Source of amusement identifies something that repeatedly entertains people.

items.example: We arrived early enough to grab a seat near the stage.
items.note: Grab a seat is informal and means sit down or secure an available seat quickly.

items.example: You can take a boat across the bay instead of driving around it.
items.note: Take a boat is a natural travel expression naming the means of transport.

items.example: In the system, each simultaneous equation relates two unknown quantities.
items.note: Simultaneous equations form a system solved together, not just any isolated equation.

items.example: The launch is on hold pending the outcome of the safety review.
items.note: Pending the outcome is formal for waiting until a process has a result.

items.example: The contract will remain unsigned pending the response from the supplier.
items.note: Pending the response means until a reply is received, often in formal communication.

items.example: The tutorial has practical value for engineers new to the system.
items.note: Practical value stresses usefulness in real situations, not merely theoretical interest.

items.example: The old photograph has sentimental value despite being inexpensive.
items.note: Sentimental value comes from emotional associations rather than market price.

items.example: The unusual design attracted attention, but much of its appeal was novelty value.
items.note: Novelty value is interest created mainly by something being new or unusual.

items.example: The company places great value on transparent communication.
items.note: Place great value on means regard a quality or thing as highly important.

items.example: The committee will assess the value of the training programme after six months.
items.note: Assess the value of means evaluate how useful, important or valuable something is.

items.example: The editor checked every quotation against a reliable source.
items.note: Reliable source stresses trustworthiness of the information provider.

items.example: The archive is a valuable source of historical records.
items.note: Valuable source emphasises how useful or important the supplied material is.

items.example: Solar heat can be a cheap source of warmth in suitable conditions.
items.note: Cheap source emphasises low cost; it does not automatically imply low quality.

items.example: The interview transcripts were a rich source of insights into user needs.
items.note: Rich source means one providing a large amount or variety of useful material.

items.example: The team identified a new source of funding for equipment purchases.
items.note: Source of funding identifies where financial support comes from.

items.example: Freelance consulting became a second source of income for her.
items.note: Source of income describes an activity or asset that brings in money.

items.example: Community theatre is a source of entertainment for local families.
items.note: Source of entertainment describes something that provides enjoyable activities.

items.example: I would jump at the chance to lead a research team overseas.
items.note: Jump at the chance shows enthusiasm for accepting an attractive opportunity.

items.example: You may get the chance to meet the author after the lecture.
items.note: Get the chance means obtain an opportunity, often by circumstance.

items.example: A proposal must meet the rules to stand a chance of being approved.
items.note: Stand a chance means have a realistic possibility of success.

items.pt: estar com chances de conseguir algo
items.example: With such strong results, the newcomer is in with a chance of winning.
items.note: Be in with a chance is especially common in British English for having a prospect of success.

items.example: Limited internet access can pose a challenge for remote teaching.
items.note: Pose a challenge describes presenting a problem that someone must overcome.

items.example: The rival's announcement represented a direct challenge to the company's strategy.
items.note: Direct challenge suggests an open, explicit threat or test of an established position.

items.example: When the deadline moved forward, the whole team rose to the challenge.
items.note: Rise to the challenge means respond competently to demanding circumstances.

items.example: Water scarcity presents a serious challenge to regional agriculture.
items.note: Serious challenge emphasises substantial difficulty or consequences.

items.example: As a child, she learned several poems by heart.
items.note: Learn by heart means memorise exactly; learn by head is not the idiomatic form.

items.example: You will miss a chance to practise speaking if you skip every discussion.
items.note: Miss a chance is idiomatic for failing to take an available opportunity.

items.example: I make an effort to review new vocabulary before each meeting.
items.note: Make an effort, not do an effort, is the usual verb-noun combination.

items.example: Can you get hold of a bilingual dictionary before the course begins?
items.note: Get hold of means find or obtain something, sometimes with difficulty.

items.example: Try to commit these useful expressions to memory through repeated practice.
items.note: Commit to memory is a fairly formal phrase meaning learn thoroughly.

items.example: Even advanced learners make mistakes with familiar word combinations.
items.note: Make mistakes is idiomatic; do mistakes is not normally used.

items.example: Do your best to speak clearly during the presentation.
items.note: Do your best means try as hard as you reasonably can.

items.example: A final review helps writers avoid mistakes in technical instructions.
items.note: Avoid mistakes is the standard combination for preventing errors.

items.example: I make a point of recording useful phrases whenever I read in English.
items.note: Make a point of followed by an -ing form expresses a deliberate regular habit.

items.example: Listen to authentic English as much as possible during the course.
items.note: As much as possible sets the greatest practical degree or frequency.

items.example: Please make a note of any collocations you want to practise again.
items.note: Make a note of means write down something to remember it.
